summary:
SUMMARIES:

Over the past 38 hours Hackathon period, our team have  developed a two-phased interactive 2D space simulation game that changes aerospace engineering and planetary exploration into a game. During Phase 1, players act as a mission designers in a garage UI (prep phase), assembling rockets from various parts while balancing strict budget, mass, power, and thrust-to-weight (TWR) constraints. While in Phase 2, after successfully launches transition into a physics-based side-scrolling rover game across procedurally generated lunar or Martian Terrain

Our project addresses the challenge pf making complex aerospace concepts accessible to the public regardless of ages. By dynamically linking the player's rocket payload such as packing a soil drill, mapping satellite, or solar panels  directly to their rover's survival and scoring capabilities, players learn firsthand how science objectives can drive spacecraft design. This is important due to the seamlessly integrated authentic NASA science facts into an engaging, visual medium, and inspiring the next generation of STEM innovators.
details:
What does it do or how does it work?

The game operates in two interconnected phases managed by persistent data sessions (MissionSession.cs).

- Phase 1 (The Garage): Players use a drag-and-drop blueprint grid to build a rocket for either a Moon or Mars landing. The game runs mathematical checks via a LaunchEvaluator to ensure the rocket has enough fuel, thrust, and parts (like heat shields for Mars) to survive.

- Phase 2 (The Surface): The game transitions to a 2D side-scrolling environment. A procedural generation algorithm builds the terrain (including lunar craters or Martian hills) and constructs a physics-driven rover at runtime based exactly on what the player packed in Phase 1. Players drive the rover, manage battery life, and collect sample or that trigger educational popups.

Our game demo (Canva)


https://canva.link/pu4eytgdoet14e6

What benefits does it have?

The primary benefit is experiential learning. Instead of reading a textbook about space exploration, players experience the consequences of engineering trade-offs. For example, if a player forgets to pack solar panels, their rover will run out of battery on the surface. If they skip the rocker-bogie suspension, their rover is much more likely to crash on rough terrain.

What is the intended impact of the project?

The intended impact is to spark interest in STEM fields by highlighting real-world space agencies' workflows. Through integrated infotainment popups, players are introduced to real NASA concepts like the Mission Design Lab (MDL), trajectory optimization (GMAT), and the harsh realities of space environments (e.g., navigating the 38% gravity of Mars or surviving two-week lunar nights).

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did we use?

- Game Engine: Unity (2D)

- Programming Language: C# (Object-Oriented Programming)

Key Frameworks:

Unity UI (Canvas Scaler, EventSystem), Unity Physics 2D (WheelJoint2D, EdgeCollider2D), Unity VideoPlayer (for .mp4 cutscenes), and TextMeshPro for crisp UI typography.

Custom Tooling:

We developed automated Unity Editor scripts (MissionGameUIBuilder, MissionGamePhase2Builder) to programmatically generate our complex UI and scene hierarchies in a single click.

How is our project creative?

Our project was heavily inspired by bridging two iconic engineering games: the complex, realistic spacecraft simulation of Kerbal Space Program (KSP) and the simplistic, physics-driven mechanical design of Bad Piggies. We took the hardcore math and orbital resource management of KSP and distilled it into an accessible Phase 1 blueprint UI, then paired it with the chaotic, side-scrolling vehicular physics of Bad Piggies for Phase 2. Furthermore, rather than pre-animating levels, our Phase2Manager uses Perlin noise and runtime instantiation to build the world from scratch every time you play, augmented by a dynamic multimedia system featuring .mp4 cutscenes and audio ducking.

What factors did our team consider?

- Educational Accuracy vs. Fun: We simplified complex delta-v calculations into "Fuel Tonnes" to keep the game accessible, while keeping the core engineering logic intact.

- UI/UX Scalability: We utilized Canvas Scalers and dynamic anchoring to ensure our HUD, blueprint grid, and popups look polished on any screen resolution.

- Code Architecture & Stability: We utilized Singleton patterns and strict component-checking algorithms to prevent overlapping runtime objects, ensuring a bug-free bridge between the rocket-building phase and the rover-driving phase.
